row: | DOC-A.1-42 | **Cultural ordering table — allowable content of the literal that identifies it**, §12.3.7 SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, GR17 (§12.3.7.4 GR17 — `ORDER TABLE ordering-name-1 IS literal-9`), conditionally required (the cultural-ordering facility is provided, A.4.9 item 11) + documented | literal-9 (an alphanumeric or national literal, or a concatenation expression of that class, never zero-length or a figurative constant — §12.3.7.3 SR10/SR11, COBOLNET0898) may name: **(1)** the ISO/IEC 14651:2020 default table **`ISO 14651_2020_TABLE1`**, matched case-insensitively with spaces and underscores interchangeable and any run of them treated as one (`iso_14651_2020_table1` is the same table) — the CLDR root collation (UCA 17.0.0) in its ISO/IEC 14651-style four-level configuration; or **(2)** as an implementor extension, a **locale tag** (`-` or `_` separators) that this implementation knows: one with a CLDR collation file of its own or of its region-less form, one with a site `.tailor` file, or a culture .NET recognizes. A `-u-co-` collation type is honoured (`de-u-co-phonebk` is German phonebook order); a locale with CLDR data takes its tailored order (`sv_SE` orders `ä` after `b`, where the default table puts it before), and a culture .NET recognizes that no collation data covers collates by the root order. Any other spelling — including another edition's table name such as `ISO 14651_2011_TABLE1` — is legal source that draws the **COBOLNET1662 warning**, and every `FUNCTION STANDARD-COMPARE` reference to that ordering-name sets **EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED** (§15.85.4 r2); with that checking off the function returns `=`. The compile-time advice and the run-time resolution are one resolver, `CollationEngine.TryGetOrderingTable` (bound in `DataBinder.OrderTableBind`). The clause is COBOL-2002 and later; below 2002 it is COBOLNET0900. | `conformance:2002/pb101_standard_compare`; `conformance:2002/pb101_ec_order_not_supported` |

row: | DOC-A.1-43 | **Currency symbol — equivalence of a currency symbol that is not a COBOL character**, §12.3.7 SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, SR20 (the equivalence) as consumed by SR21 (§12.3.7.3 SR20/SR21), required + documented | A currency symbol outside the COBOL character repertoire is equivalent to **exactly the characters that have the same .NET invariant-culture uppercase mapping** (`char.ToUpperInvariant`) and to no other character — simple case pairs, no normalization, no width folding: `é` ≡ `É`, `ω` ≡ `Ω`, full-width `ｅ` ≡ full-width `Ｅ` (but not `E`), while dotless `ı` (U+0131), which has no invariant mapping, is equivalent only to itself. Consequences: **(1)** a PICTURE character-string may write the symbol in either member of its pair — with `CURRENCY SIGN IS "é"`, `PIC É9.99` holding 1.5 edits as `é1.50`, and with `CURRENCY SIGN IS "EUR" WITH PICTURE SYMBOL "é"` as `EUR1.50` (the inserted text is always the clause's currency string as written); **(2)** two CURRENCY clauses whose symbols are equivalent but whose currency strings differ are **COBOLNET0891** (SR21) — `PICTURE SYMBOL "é"` bound to `"EUR"` and `"É"` bound to `"USD"` is refused; **(3)** the one non-COBOL character this mapping makes equivalent to a COBOL letter is `ſ` (U+017F) ≡ `S`, which is therefore a prohibited currency symbol (item 44). The same in every edition that has the clause form (the bare single-character form from COBOL-85, the PICTURE SYMBOL form from COBOL-2002). Implemented as the symbol-table key in `DataBinder.SwitchBindCurrency` and the matching in `PictureAnalyzer.Analyze`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-44 | **Currency symbol — non-COBOL characters prohibited as a currency symbol**, §8.1.2 computer's coded character set, required + documented | The compile-time coded character set is UTF-16, so it contains every non-COBOL character. **Exactly one of them is prohibited as a currency symbol: `ſ` (LATIN SMALL LETTER LONG S, U+017F)**, because its invariant uppercase is the picture letter `S` (the item-43 equivalence) and §12.3.7.3 SR22/SR27 exclude `S`; it is refused with **COBOLNET0891**, as the excluded COBOL characters are (the digits 0–9, the letters A B C D E N P R S V X Z in either case, space, and `+ - , . * / ; ( ) " =`). Every other non-COBOL character is allowed — `€`, `£`, `é`, `Ω`, `ω`, full-width letters such as `ｚ`, and full-width digits (only the ASCII digits are excluded) — in the bare single-character form and as a PICTURE SYMBOL alike, in every edition. Implemented in `DataBinder.ValidateCurrencyChar`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-51 | **DELETE FILE statement — what deleting the file does**, §14.9.10 DELETE statement, GR20 (§14.9.10.4 GR20), required + documented | A successful DELETE FILE removes **exactly one host file — the connector's resolved path — with one operating-system delete** (`File.Delete`, an unlink on POSIX hosts), for every organization: a sequential, relative or indexed physical file is one host file, and its fixed file attributes live inside it, so no sidecar, index, lock or catalog file exists to be removed (kb/Work PB802). Nothing is moved to a recycle area and nothing can be recovered by the runtime. Before deleting, the file is checked in this order: **open on this connector** → `41` and nothing is deleted (GR13); the GR18 fixed-attribute match, which never fails because the validated attribute set is empty (item 50); **held open by another file connector** of this run unit, or by any handle another process holds (tested by requesting exclusive access, so a POSIX unlink never destroys a file another run unit is reading) → `62` and the file is not deleted (GR15); **absent** → `05`, a successful completion with no action (GR14), and a bare `ASSIGN USING` connector that has never been associated is treated as absent without touching any file; present but not accessible → `37` (GR16); a medium that refuses deletion → `37` (GR17), any other host failure → `30`. On success the status is `00` and a later OPEN INPUT of the file reports `35`. Available from COBOL-2023 (COBOLNET0900 below). Implemented in `FileRegistry.DeleteFile` over `HostFile.Probe` and `HostFile.IsHeldByAnother`; the RETRY phrase's handling of the `62` conflict is item 109's. | `conformance:2023/delete_file`; `conformance:2023/delete_file_absent`; `conformance:2023/delete_file_sharing` |

row: | DOC-A.1-61 | **Dynamic-capacity table — size, location and time of physical allocation**, §8.5.1.9 dynamic-capacity tables (§8.5.1.9.1), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY — kept because it explains the cost of growth) | Each `OCCURS DYNAMIC` table is **one managed array of its own, stored outside the record that contains it** (the record holds a reference to it), so growing a table never moves or resizes its containing group. **Time and size:** the array is allocated when the containing data item is created, with room for the larger of the initial current capacity and 4 occurrences — the initial capacity being the FROM integer (or 0), raised to a table VALUE's capacity — and the initial occurrences are initialized at once. It is **reallocated only when a reference or a SET needs a higher capacity than the array holds**, by doubling (from at least 4) until it is large enough, never beyond 1,073,741,823 occurrences; newly allocated occurrences, including every intermediate one, are initialized immediately with the element's initial value (whether or not INITIALIZED is written). **Lowering the capacity** (SET … TO / DOWN BY) releases nothing physically — the slots are kept for reuse, as the §8.5.1.9.4 NOTE permits — and an occurrence re-created by a later increase is initialized afresh, never the value it held before. Implemented in `CobolDynTable` (`GrowTo`, `SetCapacity`). ⚠ An allocation the host cannot satisfy is not yet reported as EC-BOUND-TABLE-LIMIT (kb/Work PB1410, open). | — |

record.notes: VOLUNTARY row (item 61 need not be documented). §8.5.1.9.1 (cite.py --check 8.5.1.9.1 'The size, location, and time of physical allocation of a dynamic-capacity table are implementor-defined' -> OK §8.5.1.9.1 3)). Code read: CobolDynTable ctor allocates new T[Math.Max(open,4)] with open = max(FROM, VALUE capacity) and seeds via GrowTo; GrowTo doubles from >=4 capped at MaxOccurrences and seeds every new slot (i=_count..target) with _seedAt; SetCapacity shrink only lowers _count. row: | DOC-A.1-65 | **EXIT PROGRAM and GOBACK — how execution continues in a non-COBOL activating runtime element**, §14.9.18 GOBACK statement, GR1 a) (§14.9.18.4; EXIT PROGRAM reaches the same rule through §14.9.14.4 GR3), conditionally required (a .NET host can activate a COBOL.NET program) + documented | **An ordinary managed return: the host's call returns normally and the host continues at its own call site; no exception condition is raised in the host and no .NET exception is thrown to it.** The only non-COBOL activator a COBOL.NET program can have is a .NET host (a non-COBOL element cannot be the target of a CALL — item 19): the host loads the compiled assembly, calls its public `__CobolModule.Register()` once, and activates a program by name through `ProgramRegistry.CallProgram(name, callerPath, args, returning)`. When that program executes GOBACK, or EXIT PROGRAM, the generated entry (`__Activate`) catches the internal return signal and returns, so the statements after the GOBACK are not executed and the host resumes. The RETURNING item and the RAISING phrase in this case are the §3 determination 'Return to a NON-COBOL activating runtime element' (a staged RAISING condition is never raised, because the host enables no checking). Every edition. | — |

Condition met: a .NET host can activate a program.
